rows.label: Multitape implementation

quotes.text: Prima facie, it could be that Coppersmith’s algorithm is nonuniform, making it difficult to apply. For the sake of completeness, here we verify using standard ideas that Coppersmith’s algorithm can indeed be implemented to run (even on a multitape TM) in \(O(N^2\cdot\operatorname{poly}(\log N))\) time, on matrices over any field of \(\operatorname{poly}(N)\) elements. (As we work with 0-1 matrices \(A^{\prime\prime}\) and \(B^{\prime\prime}\) in our application, it suffices for us to work over a prime field of \(\operatorname{poly}(N)\) elements.)

rows.label: Polynomial evaluation, degree bounds, RS and VRS

quotes.text: Definition 4.1. Let 𝔽 be a field and S a subset of 𝔽. The evaluation of a polynomial P(x) = ∑_(i=0)^d a_i x^i over S is the function p : S → 𝔽 defined by p(s) = P(s) for all s ∈ S. The formal sum P(x) is called the polynomial corresponding to (the function) p. Similar definitions hold for multivariate polynomials.
quotes.transcription_note: Mathematical notation transcribed from the rendered page; superscripts/subscripts are written using ^ and _, fractions using parentheses, with typographic line wrapping normalized.

quotes.text:
Definition 4.2. Let 𝔽 be a field and d ≥ 0. A polynomial P (x) over 𝔽 has degree d if the
degree of P in x is at most d.

Definition 4.3. Let 𝔽 be a field, S a subset of 𝔽, and d ≥ 0. The Reed–Solomon code of
degree d over 𝔽 evaluated at S is the set of functions

RS(𝔽, S, d) := {p : S → 𝔽 s.t. p is an evaluation of a polynomial of degree at most d over S} .

Definition 4.4. Let 𝔽 be a field, S and H subsets of 𝔽, and d ≥ 0. The H-vanishing Reed–
Solomon code of degree d over 𝔽 evaluated at S is the set of functions

VRS(𝔽, S, H, d) := {p ∈ RS(𝔽, S, d) s.t. the polynomial corresponding to p vanishes on H} .
quotes.transcription_note: The wording and line wrapping of the pinned layout-text extraction are retained; blackboard field symbols are transcribed from the rendered pinned page.

rows.note: The source’s phrase “has degree d” means degree at most d (Definition 4.2). The formal functions extend from a finite evaluation set to the whole ambient field; equality is required only on the named set, as the source states.

rows.label: Fractional distance and distance to the RS code

quotes.text:
Definition 4.7. Let Σ be a finite alphabet and N a positive integer. For any two Σ-strings a and b in Σ^N, the fractional (Hamming) distance over the alphabet Σ between a and b, denoted Δ_N(a,b), is equal to the number of positions where a and b differ divided by N,
Δ_N(a,b) := |{i∈N : a_i ≠ b_i}|/N.

quotes.text:
Definition 4.8. Let 𝔽 be a field, V a subset of 𝔽, f : V → 𝔽 a univariate function, and d ≥ 0. We denote by δ_V^(d)(f) the fractional Hamming distance of f to RS(𝔽,V,d), i.e.,
δ_V^(d)(f) := inf_(P∈𝔽[x], deg_x(P)≤d) Δ_V(f,P).

rows.label: The source PCPP vocabulary and strong completeness/soundness

quotes.text: For functions r,q : ℕ → ℕ we say that a probabilistic oracle machine V is a (r,q)-PCPP verifier if, given an explicit input x = (x′,N′) with |x′| = n and oracle access to an N-bit implicit input y and proof π, V runs in time 2^(O(r(n))), tosses r(n) coins, makes q(n) queries to (y,π), and outputs either 1 (“accept”) or 0 (“reject”).
quotes.transcription_note: Mathematical notation transcribed from the rendered page; superscripts/subscripts are written using ^ and _, fractions using parentheses, with typographic line wrapping normalized.

quotes.text:
Definition 4.15. Let s ∈ (0,1] × ℕ → (0,1] and r,q : ℕ → ℕ. A pair language L belongs to the class Strong-PCP_(s(δ,n))[r(n),q(n)] if there exists a (r,q)-PCPP verifier V_L such that the following holds:
1. (Perfect) Completeness: If (x,y) ∈ L then there exists π such that Pr_R[V_L^(y,π)(x;R) = 1] = 1.
2. Soundness: For every π it holds that Pr_R[V_L^(y,π)(x;R) = 1] ≤ 1−s(Δ(y,L_x),n).

rows.label: Definition 12.14: non-adaptive PCPP verifier

quotes.text: A PCPP verifier \(V\) is non-adaptive if its queries are based only on the explicit input and its internal coin tosses, independently of the answers given to previous queries. That is, \(V\) can be decomposed into a pair of algorithms \(Q\) and \(D\) such that on explicit input \(x\) and a random tape \(r\), the verifier makes the query sequence \(Q(x,r,1),\ldots,Q(x,r,p(|x|))\), obtains the answers \(b_1,\ldots,b_{p(|x|)}\), and decides according to \(D(x,r,b_1\cdots b_{p(|x|)})\), where \(p\) is some fixed polynomial.

rows.note: FlatVerifier records the separate query and decision functions, together with randomness, query count and proof length. The 1-based concatenated input/proof indexing, the optional query value, and zero answers outside the valid domain are explicit transcription conventions; they are not extra source quotations or efficiency claims.

rows.label: Remark 12.15: field-element oracles

quotes.text: Note that the alphabet of proof oracles (as well as implicit inputs) are elements of a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\), and not bits. Thus, our descriptions of \(Q\) and \(D\) will reason about indexing into strings of such field elements. The departure from binary oracles is mostly inconsequential, with the exception of a minor note that will come up later in the proof of almost universal arguments. (See Remark 12.41.)

rows.label: Algorithm 12: V_VRS

quotes.text:
inputs:
• \(I_\ell\), irreducible polynomial of degree \(\ell\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) with root \(\mathsf{x}\), inducing the field extension \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}:=\mathbb{F}_2(\mathsf{x})\)
• \(\mathcal{B}_S\) and \(\mathcal{O}_S\), basis and offset for the \(\kappa\)-dimensional affine subspace \(S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(\mathcal{B}_H\) and \(\mathcal{O}_H\), basis and offset for the \(\lambda\)-dimensional affine subspace \(H\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(d\), positive integer indicating what “low-degree” means
randomness:
• \(r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{VRS}}(\ell,\kappa,\lambda,d)}\)
oracles:
• \(p\), function from \(S\) to \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(\pi=(\widetilde p,\widetilde\pi)\), proof of proximity to \(\mathrm{VRS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,H,d)\) for the function \(p\)

1. Proximity test of \(\widetilde p\) to \(\mathrm{RS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,d-|H|)\):
   (a) \(r'_1\cdots r'_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS}}(\ell,\kappa,d-|H|)}:=r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS}}(\ell,\kappa,d-|H|)}\)
   (b) \(b_{\mathrm{RS}}:=V_{\mathrm{RS}}^{(\widetilde p,\widetilde\pi)}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,d-|H|;r'_1\cdots r'_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS}}(\ell,\kappa,d-|H|)})\)
2. Consistency check between \(p\) and \(\widetilde p\):
   (a) \(r_1^{(\alpha)}\cdots r_\kappa^{(\alpha)}:=r_1\cdots r_\kappa\)
   (b) \(\alpha:=\operatorname{GetRandElt}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,(r_1^{(\alpha)},\ldots,r_\kappa^{(\alpha)}))\)
   (c) query \(\alpha\) to \(p\)
   (d) query \(\alpha\) to \(\widetilde p\)
   (e) \([Z_H]^{\mathsf A}:=\operatorname{FindSubspPoly}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_H,\mathcal O_H)\)
   (f) \(\omega:=[Z_H]^{\mathsf A}(\alpha)\)
   (g) if \((p(\alpha)=\omega\cdot\widetilde p(\alpha))\), then \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=1\), else \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=0\)
3. \(b:=b_{\mathrm{RS}}\wedge b_{\mathrm{consist}}\)
4. output \(b\)

notes:
• see Lemma C.5 for complexity bounds on queries and randomness
• see Lemma 12.20 for the “non-adaptive decomposition” of \(V_{\mathrm{VRS}}\) into \(Q_{\mathrm{VRS}}\) and \(D_{\mathrm{VRS}}\)
• see Algorithm 3 for \(P_{\mathrm{VRS}}\), the corresponding prover
• it must be that \(d\ge|H|\), otherwise \(p\) is certainly not in \(\mathrm{VRS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,H,d)\)

rows.label: Algorithm 13: V_RS

quotes.text:
inputs:
• \(I_\ell\), irreducible polynomial of degree \(\ell\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) with root \(\mathsf{x}\), inducing the field extension \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}:=\mathbb{F}_2(\mathsf{x})\)
• \(\mathcal{B}_S\) and \(\mathcal{O}_S\), basis and offset for the \(\kappa\)-dimensional affine subspace \(S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(d\), positive integer indicating what “low-degree” means
randomness:
• \(r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS}}(\ell,\kappa,d)}\)
oracles:
• \(p\), function from \(S\) to \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(\pi\), proof of proximity to \(\mathrm{RS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,d)\) for the function \(p\)

1. if \(\kappa\le\eta\), then:
   (a) for \(i=1,\ldots,2^\kappa\):
       i. \(\alpha_i:=\operatorname{GetEltWithIndex}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,i)\)
       ii. query \(\alpha_i\) to \(p\)
   (b) \(P:=\operatorname{SubspaceInterp}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,(p(\alpha_1),\ldots,p(\alpha_{2^\kappa})))\)
   (c) \(\widetilde d:=\deg(P)\)
   (d) if \(\widetilde d\le d\), output \(1\), else output \(0\)
2. if \(\kappa>\eta\), then:
   (a) \(d_{\kappa,\eta}:=|S|/2^\eta-1=2^\kappa/2^\eta-1\)
   (b) if \(d<d_{\kappa,\eta}\), then output \(b:=V_{\mathrm{RS},<}^{(p,\pi)}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,d;r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},<}(\ell,\kappa,d)})\)
   (c) if \(d=d_{\kappa,\eta}\), then output \(b:=V_{\mathrm{RS},=}^{(p,\pi)}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S;r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},=}(\ell,\kappa)})\)
   (d) if \(d>d_{\kappa,\eta}\), then output \(b:=V_{\mathrm{RS},>}^{(p,\pi)}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,d;r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},>}(\ell,\kappa,d)})\)

notes:
• see Lemma C.4 for complexity bounds on queries and randomness
• see Lemma 12.19 for the “non-adaptive decomposition” of \(V_{\mathrm{RS}}\) into \(Q_{\mathrm{RS}}\) and \(D_{\mathrm{RS}}\)
• see Algorithm 4 for \(P_{\mathrm{RS}}\), the corresponding prover
• if \(\kappa\le\eta\), then \(V_{\mathrm{RS}}\) can just check directly whether \(p\) is in \(\mathrm{RS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,d)\) or not

rows.label: Algorithm 14: V_RS,>

quotes.text:
inputs:
• \(I_\ell\), irreducible polynomial of degree \(\ell\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\) with root \(\mathsf{x}\), inducing the field extension \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}:=\mathbb{F}_2(\mathsf{x})\)
• \(\mathcal{B}_S\) and \(\mathcal{O}_S\), basis and offset for the \(\kappa\)-dimensional affine subset \(S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(d\), positive integer, greater than \(|S|/2^\eta-1\), indicating what “low-degree” means
randomness:
• \(r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},>}(\ell,\kappa,d)}\)
oracles:
• \(p\), function from \(S\) to \(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell}\)
• \(\pi=((p_0,\pi_0),\ldots,(p_{2^\eta-1},\pi_{2^\eta-1}))\), proof of proximity to \(\mathrm{RS}(\mathbb{F}_{2^\ell},S,d)\) for the function \(p\)

1. if \(d\ge|S|\), then output \(b:=1\)
2. if \(d<|S|\), then:
   (a) \(d_{\kappa,\eta}:=|S|/2^\eta-1=2^\kappa/2^\eta-1\)
   (b) \(m_{\kappa,\eta,d}:=\lfloor(d+1)/(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)\rfloor\)
   (c) \(r_1^{(\tau)}\cdots r_\kappa^{(\tau)}:=r_1\cdots r_\kappa\)
   (d) \(\tau:=\operatorname{GetRandElt}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,(r_1^{(\tau)},\ldots,r_\kappa^{(\tau)}))\)
   (e) query \(\tau\) to \(p\)
   (f) for \(i=0,\ldots,m_{\kappa,\eta,d}-1\):
       i. \(r_1^{(i)}\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},=}(\ell,\kappa)}^{(i)}:=r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},=}(\ell,\kappa)}\)
       ii. query \(\tau\) to \(p_i\)
       iii. \(b_i:=V_{\mathrm{RS},=}^{(p_i,\pi_i)}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,d_{\kappa,\eta};r_1^{(i)}\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},=}(\ell,\kappa)}^{(i)})\)
   (g) if \(m_{\kappa,\eta,d}\cdot(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)=d+1\), then:
       i. \(\omega_\tau:=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\tau^{i(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)}\cdot p_i(\tau)\)
       ii. if \(p(\tau)=\omega_\tau\), then \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=1\), else \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=0\)
       iii. \(b:=b_0\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}-1}\wedge b_{\mathrm{consist}}\)
       iv. output \(b\)
   (h) if \(m_{\kappa,\eta,d}\cdot(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)<d+1\), then:
       i. \(d_{\kappa,\eta,d}:=d-m_{\kappa,\eta,d}\cdot(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)\)
       ii. \(r_1^{(m_{\kappa,\eta,d})}\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},<}(\ell,\kappa,d_{\kappa,\eta,d})}^{(m_{\kappa,\eta,d})}:=r_1\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},<}(\ell,\kappa,d_{\kappa,\eta,d})}\)
       iii. \(b_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}}:=V_{\mathrm{RS},<}^{(p_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}},\pi_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}})}(I_\ell,\mathcal B_S,\mathcal O_S,d_{\kappa,\eta,d};r_1^{(m_{\kappa,\eta,d})}\cdots r_{\operatorname{rand}_{\mathrm{RS},<}(\ell,\kappa,d_{\kappa,\eta,d})}^{(m_{\kappa,\eta,d})})\)
       iv. query \(\tau\) to \(p_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}}\)
       v. \(\omega_\tau:=\sum_{i=0}^{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}}\tau^{i(d_{\kappa,\eta}+1)}\cdot p_i(\tau)\)
       vi. if \(p(\tau)=\omega_\tau\), then \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=1\), else \(b_{\mathrm{consist}}:=0\)
       vii. \(b:=b_0\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}-1}\wedge b_{m_{\kappa,\eta,d}}\wedge b_{\mathrm{consist}}\)
       viii. output \(b\)

rows.label: The reconstruction problem

quotes.text:
Recall that we wish to solve the following problem:
Given: An oracle \(f:F^m\to F\) and parameters \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}\).
Goal: Reconstruct (an implicit representation for) every polynomial of total degree at most \(d\) that has \(\varepsilon\)-agreement with the function \(f\). Specifically, construct randomized oracle machines \(M_1,\ldots,M_l\) such that for every polynomial \(p:F^m\to F\) of degree \(d\) that has (relative) agreement \(\varepsilon\) with \(f\), there exists \(j\in[l]\) such that \(M_j^f\) computes \(p\).

rows.label: Definition 20: computation and agreement

quotes.text: A randomized procedure \(A\) is said to compute a function \(f:X\to Y\) at a point \(x\in X\) if \(\Pr[A(x)=f(x)]\ge3/4\), where the probability is taken over the internal coin tosses of \(A\). We say that \(A\) has agreement \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) with \(f\) if \(A\) computes \(f\) on an \(\alpha\) fraction of the inputs in \(X\). We say that \(A\) computes \(f\) if it has agreement \(1\) with \(f\). A randomized procedure \(A\) is said to solve a search problem \(S\), if on input \(x\), \(\Pr[A(x)\in S(x)]\ge3/4\).

quotes.text: Thus we will assume we have oracle access to the received word \(r\) (the input). We will also output the codewords implicitly, by programs that compute the function represented by the codeword. These programs will be allowed to make oracle calls to the received word \(r\). Thus both our decoding algorithm and their output programs are best thought of as oracle-machines. We will use the notation \(M^{\mathcal{O}}(x)\) to denote the computation of an oracle-machine \(M\) on input \(x\) with access to an oracle \(\mathcal{O}\). When asking for efficient list-decoding, we will expect that the decoding algorithm, as well as its output programs are all efficient.

quotes.locator: Definition 20 (Probabilistic Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCP of proximity, or PCPP))
quotes.revision: CCC 2019, LIPIcs 137, article 19, published Dagstuhl version
quotes.text:
For \(s,\delta : \mathbb{N} \to [0,1]\) and \(r,q : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), a verifier \(V\) is a PCP of proximity system for a pair language \(L\) with proximity parameter \(\delta\), soundness parameter \(s\), number of random bits \(r\) and query complexity \(q\) if the following holds for all \(x,y\):

If \((x,y) \in L\), there is a proof \(\pi\) such that \(V(x)\) accepts oracle \(y \circ \pi\) with probability 1.

If \(y\) is \(\delta(|x|)\)-far from \(L(x) := \{z : (x,z) \in L\}\), then for all proofs \(\pi\), \(V(x)\) accepts oracle \(y \circ \pi\) with probability at most \(s(|x|)\).

\(V(x)\) tosses \(r(|x|)\) random coins, and makes at most \(q(|x|)\) non-adaptive queries.

rows.label: The cited polynomial-time verifier convention

quotes.revision: January 2006 author full version; not the SIAM typeset version
quotes.text:
A verifier is a probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm \(V\) that, on an input \(x\) of length \(n\), tosses \(r = r(n)\) random coins \(R\) and generates a sequence of \(q = q(n)\) queries \(I = (i_1,\ldots,i_q)\) and a circuit \(D : \{0,1\}^q \to \{0,1\}\) of size at most \(d(n)\).

We think of \(V\) as representing a probabilistic oracle machine that queries its oracle \(\pi\) for the positions in \(I\), receives the \(q\) answer bits \(\pi|_I \triangleq (\pi_{i_1},\ldots,\pi_{i_q})\), and accepts iff \(D(\pi|_I) = 1\).

We write \((I,D) \overset{R}{\leftarrow} V(x)\) to denote the queries and circuit generated by \(V\) on input \(x\) and random coin tosses, and \((I,D) = V(x;R)\) if we wish to specify the coin tosses \(R\).
